title: Round Hill is suing Suno and Anthropic for up to $1B apiece. It isn’t looking to settle.

reading.body:
The failure here sits at the data-collection stage of model development. Suno admitted its model was trained on what it described as essentially all music files on the internet, and reporting based on a hack identified YouTube, Deezer, and Genius among the scraping sources. The labels demonstrated that the trained system could reproduce recognizable versions of specific copyrighted recordings when prompted, which places the problem not only in training-data acquisition but also in the model's outputs, where protected expression surfaced in generated content available to any paying user.

This is a case of a system deployed publicly without mechanisms to prevent reproduction of copyrighted source material, either at the point of data ingestion or at the point of generation. No licensing agreements with rights-holders were in place before deployment. Catching it earlier would have required either clearing rights before training, filtering copyrighted works from training corpora, or testing outputs systematically against protected recordings before public release. None of those steps is established to have occurred.

What is not established is that deliberate intent to infringe has been proven as a legal finding. Lawsuits, class actions, and one German court ruling against Suno are part of the record, and Warner Music reached a settlement with Suno, but the bulk of the litigation in the United States remains unresolved, and allegations in complaints are not verdicts.

summary:
Major record labels, including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, Warner Music, Capitol Records, and Atlantic Records, have filed separate lawsuits against Udio and Suno, two popular AI music generators. The labels accuse both companies of scraping massive amounts of copyrighted music without permission and directly reproducing sections of famous songs in their AI-generated outputs. The lawsuits claim the companies deliberately concealed what music they used for training their models, though both previously claimed their use of copyrighted material constituted fair use.

To support their case, the record labels created AI-generated songs using specific prompts and demonstrated they could reproduce versions of famous works by artists including The Beatles, Frank Sinatra, Bruce Springsteen, Michael Jackson, and Mariah Carey. They submitted thousands of copyrighted works they claim were scraped for training data, along with a thumb drive of AI-generated examples showing similarities to originals. The lawsuits target both companies and unnamed individuals who allegedly helped scrape the music, setting up a major legal battle over how generative AI services handle copyrighted material.
